transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thank you. Um, well, I guess I'm here because I’m just—I’m honestly at my wit's end with myself at work. I work in video production, mostly as a camera operator and an editor, which I’ve been doing for years, ever since I got my degree. So I know what I'm doing, you know? I really, really do. But it's getting to a point where it finally scared me into actually making an appointment and coming in today, because I just keep making these completely dumb technical mistakes. 

And it’s so incredibly frustrating because I *know* better. I know exactly how to do my job, but I’ll do things like label the camera cards wrong after a long shoot, which is a huge deal when you're handing media off to a post-house. Or I'll be in the editing bay and just completely miss a timecode note from the director, even though it's sitting right there in my notes. 

The thing that really sent me into a panic, though, was the other day when I was finishing up a project. I exported a final client cut, and it had the completely wrong lower-third graphic on it. Just the wrong name and title under the person speaking. And the crazy thing is, I checked it! I literally sat there, watched the sequence down, checked the export, looked right at the screen, and I *still* missed it. It went to the client like that. It's just so embarrassing, and honestly, in this industry, you make a few of those careless mistakes and people just stop calling you for gigs, so I really need to figure out why my brain keeps skipping over these details when I'm looking right at them.
Do you find yourself making similar mistakes or overlooking details in your personal life outside of work?

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because I’ve actually tried to figure that out myself, and... not really? I honestly don't think I do. It’s so weird. Like, at home, my life is just—well, it's structured so differently. I don't really have those same high-stakes, detail-oriented tasks sitting in front of me. I mean, if I'm cooking, which I actually do a lot to unwind after a long shoot day, I'm just kind of throwing things in a pan. I never measure anything anyway, so if I miss a step in a recipe, it just means dinner tastes a little different, it's not a mistake that ruins everything. 

And I’m pretty good about the important stuff at home. Like, I have a cat, Barnaby—he’s this incredibly needy orange tabby I rescued a few years ago—and he has this very specific medication schedule for his thyroid, and I never, ever mess that up. I am totally dialed in on his routine. I pay my rent, I keep my personal life pretty functional... so no, I really don't notice myself overlooking things outside of my job. 

Which honestly just makes the work stuff even more maddening! Because why can I perfectly manage Barnaby’s pill schedule and remember exactly where I put my spare keys at home, but then I sit down in the editing bay and completely glaze over a glaring typo on a client's name? It just feels like my brain selectively betrays me only when my actual livelihood is on the line, you know? So yeah, it really just seems confined to when I'm on the clock.
Do you feel overwhelmed or anxious when you're working on projects, especially when there are deadlines to meet?

Oh, overwhelmed? Anxious? You know, it's—it's complicated, I guess. Because, okay, so deadlines are just the reality of video production. Like, you never *don't* have a deadline. Whether it's the director breathing down your neck to get the rough cut out by Friday, or you're on set and you only have the location permitted until 6 PM and the sun is literally going down while you're trying to get the last shot... deadlines are just the air we breathe in this industry. 

So, I don't know if I'd call it anxiety, exactly? It's more like... this intense, buzzing energy. Like, when a deadline is coming up fast, I actually kind of get into this weird zone. My heart beats faster, sure, and maybe I'm a little stressed, but it's almost like a high. I'll be bouncing my leg under the editing desk, clicking through the timeline a mile a minute, just *going*. I don't freeze up or get paralyzed by panic, if that's what you mean. I just get really, really amped up. 

But the overwhelming part... yeah, maybe. Because when I'm in that state, when I'm just rushing and buzzing and trying to beat the clock, that's usually when the mistakes happen. It's like my brain is moving so fast that my eyes can't keep up, or my hands are moving faster than my thoughts. I'm just pushing buttons and dragging clips and trying to get it done, done, done. And then I hit export, and I'm like, "Whew, made it!" and then... boom. Wrong graphic. Wrong timecode. 

So I don't sit there worrying and chewing my nails, feeling anxious in that way. It's more like I'm a runaway train when the pressure is on. I just go too fast, and I can't seem to put the brakes on to actually look at what I'm doing. Does that make sense? It's like the deadline gives me all this frantic energy, but no steering wheel.
Do you notice any physical symptoms, like headaches or stomach issues, when you're in that frantic, high-energy state while working under deadlines?

Physical symptoms? Um... like headaches or stomach stuff? You know, I don't really think so. I mean, obviously, if I've been staring at a monitor for, like, fourteen hours straight, my eyes will burn, and maybe I'll get a little bit of a tension headache right at the base of my skull, but that's just from the glare and sitting in a dark bay all day, not from the frantic energy itself. But stomach issues? No, definitely not. I actually have a pretty iron stomach. I mean, on set, you're eating craft services—which is basically just a mountain of gummy bears, stale bagels, and whatever weird catering they dragged in at 5 AM—and I can eat all of that and be totally fine. Even when we're rushing to get a shot before we lose the light, and I'm practically running with a thirty-pound camera rig on my shoulder, my stomach is completely fine. 

Actually, if anything, when I'm in that super amped-up state, I kind of forget I even have a body? Like, I'll realize at 4 PM that I haven't had a sip of water or gone to the bathroom since breakfast because I've just been so locked into that high-speed buzzing mode. So it's not that my body is reacting badly with pain or sickness, it's more like my brain just unplugs from my physical self entirely while I'm racing against the clock. So yeah, no stomach aches or stress headaches or anything like that. Just the usual physical exhaustion that comes with the territory of production work, you know? But nothing that spikes specifically when I'm rushing to meet a deadline.
Do you ever feel a sense of dread before starting a new project at work?

Dread? Oh, wow. Um. No, I wouldn't call it dread. Honestly, it's almost the exact opposite? Like, starting a new project is probably my favorite part of the whole process. I love that initial phase. It's so exciting! You get the creative brief, or you have that first kickoff meeting with the director and the producers, and everyone is throwing out ideas, and it's all just... potential, you know? 

Like, last month, we started this documentary project about urban beekeepers—which, by the way, is a wild subculture, I had no idea people were keeping thousands of bees on top of apartment buildings in the city—but anyway, when we first started, I was so pumped. I was researching different lenses we could use to get macro shots of the honeycombs, and I was pulling all these visual references, and building these elaborate mood boards. I get so invested in the shiny newness of it all. 

There's no dread at all when things are fresh. I'm usually the one who's most energized in the room on day one. I'm practically bouncing in my chair, ready to just dive in and shoot. The dread—if you can even call it that, maybe it's more like a heavy, dragging feeling—that doesn't show up until way, way later. Like, weeks into post-production when the novelty has completely worn off, and I'm staring at the same thirty seconds of footage for the fiftieth time, trying to perfectly match the audio levels of a guy talking about pollen. That's when I start feeling like, "Ugh, I can't do this anymore." But the beginning? No, the beginning is the best part. I never dread starting something new. If anything, I probably start too many new things because I just love that initial rush of a fresh idea so much.
Do you ever find yourself putting off or avoiding certain tasks at work?

Putting off tasks? Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. All the time. But, see, it's not the fun stuff. Like I said, the shooting, the brainstorming, the initial assembly of a rough cut—I'm all over that. I will do that immediately. But there's this whole other side to my job that is just... tedious. Mind-numbingly tedious. 

Like, logging footage. Oh my god, logging footage is the bane of my existence. When you come back from a shoot, especially a documentary shoot where you've been rolling for six hours straight, you have to go through and log every single clip. You have to label it, add metadata, write little descriptions like "wide shot of beekeeper walking left to right," mark the good takes, sync the external audio... it is so boring. It's just sitting there, typing data into a spreadsheet or a bin in Premiere. And I will do literally anything to avoid it. 

I'll tell myself, "Okay, I'll log the footage right after I organize my desk." And then I'm organizing my desk, and I find an old hard drive, and I'm like, "Oh, I should check what's on this." And then an hour goes by, and I'm looking at footage from a project three years ago. Or I'll decide that before I can log the footage, I absolutely need to update all my software plugins, which of course takes forever and requires a restart. I just keep finding these little side quests to go on. 

And it's not just logging. It's the paperwork, too. Expense reports! I am notoriously terrible at expense reports. I'll have a stack of crumpled receipts from gear rentals and coffee runs shoved in the bottom of my camera bag for weeks. Production managers are always chasing me down, sending me these passive-aggressive emails like, "Hey, just a friendly reminder that your expenses from the shoot last month are past due." And every time I get one of those emails, I'm like, "I know, I know, I'll do it today," but then I just... don't. I'll open the expense portal, look at the blank fields, and suddenly I feel this overwhelming urge to go get a snack, or check my email, or literally just stare at the wall. 

It's like there's a physical wall between me and the boring tasks. I know I have to do them. I know it's part of the job. But I just keep pushing them off until the very last possible second, usually until someone is actually mad at me, or I physically cannot proceed with the edit until the footage is logged. And then I have to do it in a complete panic, which goes back to that whole frantic energy thing. But yeah, if a task doesn't have a creative spark or an immediate deadline attached to it, I will avoid it like the plague.
Do you think your mistakes at work or your avoidance of certain tasks have affected your relationships with your colleagues or supervisors?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, it definitely has. And honestly, it’s been really stressing me out lately because... well, it's becoming kind of obvious. I can tell my producers have started trusting me less, especially when it comes to the really complex shoots. You know, the ones where we have multiple company moves in a single day, or intricate lighting setups where we have to coordinate with, like, three different departments and stick to a ridiculously tight schedule. They used to just hand me the call sheet and let me run with it, but lately, they've been assigning a junior producer to basically shadow me, or they’ll give the lead camera position to someone else entirely, even if I've been on the project longer. 

And the thing that drives me absolutely crazy—like, it genuinely keeps me up at night—is that my actual camera work is fantastic. I know I'm good at what I do. When I'm behind the lens, my framing is spot on, my handheld work is super smooth, I know exactly how to pull focus on the fly. Directors always love the footage I get! They're constantly complimenting my eye. So it’s not the art, you know? It’s not the technical skill of operating the camera. 

But because I'm always late with the paperwork, or I put off logging the footage until it bottlenecks the whole post-production pipeline, or I miss an email about a gear swap because I was avoiding my inbox... it’s taking a real toll. I’ve been trying to move up to a senior Director of Photography role for the last year and a half. I’ve had all these meetings about it, and I really thought I was next in line. But now? I can feel that chance just completely slipping away. 

It’s like the supervisors look at me and think, "Sure, she gets beautiful shots, but can we trust her to manage an entire camera department and handle the logistics without dropping the ball?" And right now, they clearly don't think they can. Which is just... it’s so frustrating. I have the creative vision for it, I really do, but I just can't seem to get the organized, administrative side of my brain to cooperate, and it's definitely damaging my reputation. I mean, just last week my line producer pulled me aside and gave me this whole lecture about "reliability" which was just mortifying. So, yeah... it's definitely affecting my relationships with them. A lot more than I'd like to admit.
How do you feel when your supervisors or colleagues criticize your work or point out your mistakes?

How do I feel? Um. I mean, I’m not entirely sure how to answer that, to be honest. I don't know if I have a specific... reaction, really? Like, I haven't really noticed a pattern other than just, you know, normal frustration? 

Take that lecture from my line producer last week. We were standing right by the craft services table, and I was just trying to grab a coffee before we had to move the whole B-roll setup to a different location across town, and he just pulls me aside and starts in on the whole "reliability" thing. And in my head, I'm just thinking about the fifty other things I need to be doing, but I'm standing there listening to him point out that I missed the gear swap email. And it's like, I want to explain to him *why* I missed it—because that email was buried in a thread that originally started out being about the catering budget, which I have absolutely nothing to do with, so of course I stopped reading it! But if I say that, it just sounds like an excuse, right? 

So I usually just stand there and nod and try to get through the conversation as fast as humanly possible so I can get back to actually shooting. Because it’s never my creative work they’re criticizing. If a director came up to me and said, "Hey, your framing on that last shot was terrible," I would probably be devastated. Like, genuinely crushed. But when it's about the paperwork or the logging or being late on an expense report... I don't know. I guess I just feel kind of flustered? Or annoyed that we're even talking about it when there's actual, tangible creative work to be done? 

I know they're right, obviously, I know I dropped the ball, but I just want them to understand the context, you know? It's not like I'm doing it on purpose. But yeah, I don't really know if I have a specific way I feel about it overall. I mean, what do you mean exactly? Like, are you asking if I get mad at them? Because I don't really get mad, I just... I don't know. I'm not really sure what you're looking for there.
Do you feel upset or emotional when your supervisors or colleagues point out your mistakes?

Upset? Emotional? No... I don't think so. I mean, I don't go cry in the bathroom or anything like that. It's not like I'm tearing up when the line producer is lecturing me by the craft services table. Like I was just trying to say, it's more just... an annoyance? A frustration? Because to me, getting emotional implies that my feelings are deeply hurt, and my feelings aren't hurt when someone tells me I forgot to submit a receipt for a lens rental or that I'm bottlenecking the post-production pipeline. It's just logistics! Why would I cry over a spreadsheet? 

Now, if they told me my lighting was flat, or my color grading was totally washed out on a project I spent three weeks on—okay, yes, then I would be emotional. I would probably be an absolute wreck. I remember this one time, maybe five or six years ago, a director told me my handheld work was too shaky during this really intense, quiet scene we were shooting in this tiny, cramped apartment. And I was so upset I literally couldn't sleep that entire night. I just kept replaying the shot in my head, over and over, thinking about how I could have stabilized my stance better, or maybe used an entirely different shoulder rig, or if I should have just suggested we put it on sticks even though he wanted that gritty documentary feel... but see, that's because I care about the art. The art is my life. 

But the paperwork? The emails? The logging? No, I don't get emotional about that. I just get... I don't know, defensive, maybe? Because I just want to yell, "Look at the footage! The footage is gorgeous! Who cares if the metadata is a day late!" I mean, I know they care, and I know it's a business, but I just can't bring myself to feel heartbroken over an expense report. So, no, I wouldn't use the word 'emotional.' I'm just trying to survive the boring stuff so I can get back behind the camera. Does that make sense? I just don't think 'upset' is the right word for it at all.
Have you ever felt like your mistakes or difficulties at work were significantly impacting your overall well-being or ability to function in your daily life?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, I think I kind of touched on this earlier, but it’s just... it’s a massive weight on me right now. Because, like I was saying before about how my producers have started trusting me less on those really complex shoots? That doesn't just stay at work, you know? It completely follows me home. I’ll be sitting in my apartment at, like, eleven at night, trying to unwind, maybe trying to watch a movie, but I can't even focus on the cinematography because I'm just obsessing over the fact that they gave the lead camera position to someone else that day. It completely ruins my evening. I just sit there thinking about how hard I've worked for the last decade, hauling heavy gear in the freezing rain, pulling sixteen-hour days on tiny indie sets, all to build up the trust to run a big crew, and now they're second-guessing me. 

And then there’s the promotion thing. Like I mentioned, my chance at moving into a senior Director of Photography role has just been slipping away, and that... that honestly messes with my head on a daily basis. It really impacts my overall well-being because being a DP isn't just a job title for me, it's my entire identity. I’ve been building my reel for years for this specific bump up. And knowing that my actual camera work is top-tier, knowing that I have the exact creative eye they need, but I'm still losing out on my dream job just because I can't keep my inbox organized or I'm late filing a stupid location release... it’s maddening. 

It makes me feel so stuck in my daily life. I wake up in the morning and I just feel this heavy, exhausting dread, wondering if today is the day they officially give the DP slot to that guy from the B-unit who shoots completely uninspired, flat video but always has his timesheets turned in on Friday at 5 PM sharp. It's like I'm watching my own career derail in slow motion and I can't figure out how to pull the emergency brake. So, yeah, even though I don't get teary-eyed over the spreadsheets themselves, the *consequences* of all this stuff... the loss of trust from the producers, the stalled career despite the quality of my footage... it definitely takes a huge toll on my life outside of just being on set. I just can't seem to shake it off when I go home.
Do you feel like your difficulties at work are affecting your relationships or daily activities outside of work?

Relationships? Um... I mean, no, not really? Because, honestly, I don't really have much of a social life to begin with, to be completely frank with you. Like, the film and TV industry is just so all-consuming. When you're pulling twelve, fourteen, sometimes sixteen-hour days on set, there isn't really a lot of time left over to go to brunch or join a book club or do whatever normal people do on the weekends. My friends are pretty much all crew members anyway—the grips, the gaffers, the other camera ops. So when we do manage to grab a drink after wrap, we just talk about work. It's not like my work problems are ruining my relationships with them, because they totally get it. They know exactly which producers are breathing down my neck about timesheets or whatever, so we just vent about it. 

And as for daily activities outside of work... I mean, what even *are* my daily activities? I go home, I order Thai food, I maybe put on a Criterion Collection Blu-ray to study the cinematography, and I pass out. Like I was saying before, I might sit there obsessing over the job and feeling that dread, but it's not stopping me from... I don't know, living my life? I guess you could ask if it stops me from doing chores or something, but honestly, I'm always behind on my laundry anyway. That's just because I'm physically exhausted from carrying a thirty-pound camera rig all day, not because I'm too upset about work to fold my shirts. 

So, no, I wouldn't say it's affecting my relationships or my day-to-day stuff. I'm just living the exact same chaotic freelancer life I've always lived, just with this extra layer of frustration about the DP promotion sitting in the back of my head. But my actual activities? Nah, they're pretty much exactly the same as they've always been. Wait, what did you mean by daily activities, anyway? Like going to the gym? Because I haven't been to the gym in months, but again, that's just the schedule, you know? I don't think I really have anything to report on that front.
Do you feel like your work difficulties are significantly impacting your ability to enjoy or participate in activities you normally like to do?

Activities I normally like to do... huh. I mean, not really? Because, well, like I was saying, my life is mostly film anyway. So the things I do for fun are usually just... more camera stuff. Like, okay, for example, a few weeks ago I bought this old, beat-up Soviet anamorphic lens on eBay—it has this incredible, swirly bokeh that you just can't replicate with modern digital lenses. Anyway, it arrived and it was full of fungus, which happens a lot with those old lenses from the seventies, so I spent an entire Sunday afternoon just sitting at my kitchen table, taking it completely apart, cleaning every single glass element, re-greasing the focus ring, and putting it all back together. And I loved it! I had the absolute best time doing that. 

So, no, the stress about the paperwork or the DP promotion didn't stop me from enjoying that at all. I wasn't sitting there staring at the lens barrel stressing out about my timesheets or the line producer. I mean, sure, maybe I'll think about the promotion *after* I'm done, or when I'm trying to fall asleep, like I mentioned before, but the actual enjoyment of the activity itself? No, that's completely intact. Because the camera stuff is my passion, you know? It’s why I got into this insane business in the first place. If anything, doing those things—tinkering with gear, or watching a really beautifully shot foreign film—that's my escape from all the logistical nightmares and the emails. It's like my sanctuary. 

So I definitely wouldn't say the work difficulties are ruining my hobbies or my ability to have fun. I still get that exact same spark, that same rush, when I fix a piece of gear or when I go out and shoot some test footage in the park with a new filter. I just... I just wish I had more hours in the day to do it, honestly. But that's just the nature of the industry, right? It totally eats your time, but it hasn't eaten my actual enjoyment of the things I love doing. So, yeah, no impact on the enjoyment part. I'm still me in that regard.
Do you often feel guilty or self-critical about your mistakes at work?

Guilty? Um... no. I really wouldn't use the word guilty. Or self-critical, really. I mean, okay, if I blew a focus pull on a really crucial, emotional take where the lead actor just gave the performance of a lifetime? Yeah, absolutely, I would beat myself up over that for weeks. I'd be incredibly self-critical because that's the art, you know? That's the actual job. But the mistakes we've been talking about? The administrative stuff? The unread emails or the late timesheets? No, I don't feel guilty about those at all. 

Because, honestly... and I don't want to sound arrogant here, but I just don't think they're that important in the grand scheme of what we're trying to achieve on set. Like, picture this: we're on location, the sun is going down, we're losing daylight fast, and the director is practically having a panic attack because we have exactly four minutes of magic hour left to get the most important shot of the entire film. My entire brain, my entire physical being, is focused on framing that shot, communicating with my 1st AC, keeping the rig steady... I'm literally making the movie. So if I forget to hand in a petty cash receipt for a fifteen-dollar roll of pink gaffer tape because I was busy saving the production's ass, why should I feel guilty? 

It's just so frustrating because the line producers sit in their climate-controlled trailers, staring at their little Excel grids, and they treat a missing signature on a location release like it's some sort of cardinal sin. They have absolutely no idea what it actually takes to get the footage in the can when you're out there in the mud. So, no, I don't sit at home feeling guilty or criticizing myself for not being good at paperwork. I feel angry, sure. I feel incredibly annoyed that the system is set up to punish creatives for not being accountants. But I don't look in the mirror and think I'm a failure. I know my worth on set. I know my eye is good. So, yeah, no guilt here. Just... just a lot of frustration that they can't see past the administrative chaos to see the actual value I'm bringing to the screen. Does that make sense? Like, why should I feel bad about something that has absolutely nothing to do with my actual skill as a filmmaker?
Do you feel like your mistakes at work are reflecting poorly on you as a person?

Reflecting poorly on me as a *person*? No, definitely not. I mean, I guess it depends on how you define what makes a person good or bad, right? Because to me, my character is about my dedication to the craft, my loyalty to my crew, my artistic integrity. Like, if I'm on set and a grip drops a fifty-pound sandbag on his foot, I'm the first one dropping what I'm doing to make sure he's okay. If the director needs a sounding board because the lead actress is throwing a tantrum in her trailer and refusing to come out, I'm the one talking him off the ledge and figuring out how we can shoot the B-roll in the meantime so we don't fall behind schedule. That's who I am. That's my personality and my character. 

So no, the fact that I can't seem to remember to log my meal penalties on a piece of paper or that I constantly forget to reply to the production coordinator's emails doesn't make me feel like a bad person. It makes me feel like a disorganized person, sure, or maybe a person who would absolutely fail at a corporate desk job, but I already knew that! That's exactly why I went to film school and not business school, you know? 

I just... I really separate the two things in my head. There's the administrative bureaucracy, which is just this completely arbitrary system invented by studios and insurance companies to cover their own bases, and then there's the actual human element of making art with a team of people. My mistakes are entirely in that first category. The paperwork category. And honestly, if a producer thinks I'm a fundamentally flawed human being because I didn't CC them on an email about a lens rental, then that's their problem, not mine. They're the ones who are completely lacking perspective. Because at the end of the day, when you're sitting in a dark theater watching the final cut of the movie, you're not looking at the timesheets. You're looking at the lighting, the framing, the emotion on the screen. And I know I deliver on that front. I pour my absolute soul into the images I capture. So, no, I don't let the administrative slip-ups touch my actual self-worth as a human being. I just don't.
Do you feel like your difficulties at work are affecting your overall sense of identity or self-worth?

Affecting my identity? No, definitely not. I mean, it's kind of like what I was just saying about being a good person, right? My identity is completely, one hundred percent wrapped up in being a cinematographer. It's who I am down to my bones. Like, if you ask me who I am at a dinner party—which, by the way, I usually hate dinner parties because people always ask the most boring, surface-level questions—but if you did, I wouldn't say, 'Hi, I'm an employee who meticulously files expense reports.' I'd say, 'I'm a filmmaker.' And that identity is bulletproof, honestly. 

Because I know what I can do with a camera. Like, just last month, we were shooting this indie short—super low budget, basically paying for our own craft services, total passion project—and the director wanted this incredibly complex tracking shot. We had to follow the lead actor through a crowded diner, out the back door, down an alley, and into a moving car. The producer was sweating bullets, looking at his watch, telling us we didn't have the time or the expensive Steadicam gear to pull it off. But I just saw the whole sequence in my head. I knew exactly how the light was going to hit the actor's face when he pushed through the diner doors. So I rigged up this makeshift gimbal with some spare parts I had in my trunk, strapped it to myself, and we nailed it in three takes. Three takes! When you can do something like that, when you can literally pull magic out of thin air and capture it on a sensor... that's your identity. That's your self-worth right there. 

So the fact that I got an absolutely scathing email the next day because I didn't submit the equipment manifest on the right color-coded portal? I mean, it's annoying, it's incredibly frustrating, and yeah, it might cost me that DP promotion on the bigger union shoot, which totally sucks and stresses me out, but it doesn't make me question who I am. I know I'm a great camera operator. I know my eye is undeniable. The administrative stuff is just... it's just noise. It's this loud, obnoxious, bureaucratic noise that gets in the way of the actual art, but it's not *me*. I am not my unread emails. I'm the images I create. 

So, yeah, my self-worth is completely intact. It's the industry's priorities that are completely messed up, if you ask me. Because if they actually valued the final product over the paperwork, they wouldn't care how many times I forgot to log a meal penalty. They'd just look at the dailies and say, 'Wow, she really nailed that shot.' But they don't, they obsess over the margins, and it's just—I don't know, it's like trying to judge a painter by how neatly they organize their paint tubes instead of looking at the actual canvas. It just doesn't make any sense to me to let that define how I feel about myself.
Do you often feel sad or depressed?

Sad? Depressed? Um... no. Not really. I mean, sure, I have bad days like anybody else, but it's never that heavy, can't-get-out-of-bed kind of sadness, you know? I think my brain is just moving way too fast for that. If I'm upset about something, it usually manifests as, like, intense frustration or just being incredibly keyed up and annoyed. 

Like, just last week, the grip truck got a flat tire on the way to this location out in the middle of nowhere, and we lost three hours of shooting time. Three hours! On a twelve-hour day, that is an absolute lifetime. But I wasn't sitting on an apple box crying about it or feeling hopeless. I was pacing around this dirt parking lot, practically vibrating with energy, trying to figure out how we could re-block the entire afternoon to make up for the lost time. I was calling the rental house, I was sketching out new lighting diagrams on the back of a call sheet, I was—well, I was yelling at the production manager a little bit, which, okay, maybe wasn't my most professional moment, but I was just so fired up! 

So, yeah, "depressed" just isn't the right word for me at all. I honestly think you have to be able to slow down to be depressed, right? And I don't really slow down. I'm always onto the next shot, the next problem to solve, the next setup. Even when I get home after a fourteen-hour day and my body is just physically destroyed from carrying a camera on my shoulder, my mind is still racing. I'm thinking about what lenses we need for tomorrow, or how I'm going to expose for that tricky interior scene where the windows are blowing out. There's just no room in there for sadness.
